title: Indigenous Cultural Safety: Address Racism, Power, and Access—Not Stereotypes
bottomLine: Culturally safe Indigenous health care is defined by the patient's experience and requires attention to colonial harms, anti-Indigenous racism, power imbalance, access barriers and individual identity. Do not substitute population stereotypes, pan-Indigenous assumptions or ceremonial checklists for person-centred care.
recognize: Prior experiences of racism, forced relocation, residential schools, child welfare, coerced treatment and unsafe care can shape trust and access across generations without determining any individual patient's beliefs.
differentiate: Cultural awareness describes clinician knowledge; cultural safety requires the care relationship and system to reduce power-based harm and discrimination.
assessment: Ask the patient how they identify, what matters in care, who they want involved, whether language or cultural supports are desired and what barriers make the plan difficult.
workup: Use the same evidence-based diagnostic standards while recognizing that unequal access and prior dismissal can cause delayed presentation; do not lower diagnostic vigilance because symptoms are attributed to social stereotypes.
management: Provide equitable evidence-based treatment, offer Indigenous patient navigator, Elder or traditional healing supports when desired, and address transportation, medication access and continuity barriers.
medicationSafety: Do not assume use of traditional medicines; ask respectfully about all medicines and assess interactions without dismissing cultural practices.
redFlags: Coercion or exclusion of chosen supports
Unsafe discharge caused by access barriers
counselling: Acknowledge uncertainty and past harm when relevant, avoid demanding disclosure of trauma, and ask what would make care safer.
followUp: Close referral and result loops because fragmented access can amplify inequity.
examTrap: Choosing a treatment based on a stereotype about what Indigenous patients value rather than asking the individual patient.
oneLinePearl: Cultural safety is not knowing a culture—it is creating care the patient experiences as safe and equitable.
sourceBasis: Canadian nursing cultural-safety and anti-racism standards

title: 2SLGBTQIA+ Care: Anatomy, Goals, and Respectful Questions
system: Professional Practice / Equity / Sexual and Gender Health
bottomLine: High-quality 2SLGBTQIA+ care uses affirmed name and pronouns, asks anatomy and sexual practices only when clinically relevant, and bases screening and treatment on organs, exposures, hormones and individual risk rather than gender assumptions.
recognize: Gender identity, sex assigned at birth, sexual orientation, anatomy and sexual practices are distinct clinical variables.
differentiate: A transgender man may still need cervical screening if a cervix is present; a transgender woman may have prostate-related disease depending on anatomy and treatment history.
assessment: Ask affirmed name/pronouns, relevant organs, hormone or surgery history, sexual practices/exposure sites, fertility goals and experiences of discrimination only to the degree needed for care.
workup: Apply organ- and risk-based screening; test STI exposure sites based on practices rather than identity labels.
management: Provide routine primary and specialty care without forcing patients into gendered pathways; coordinate gender-affirming therapy with preventive and chronic disease needs.
medicationSafety: Gender-affirming hormones have monitoring and interaction considerations but should not be stopped reflexively during unrelated illness without a clinical reason.
redFlags: Discrimination causing avoidance of urgent care
counselling: Do not make fertility assumptions; offer preservation and pregnancy prevention discussions based on reproductive potential and goals.
followUp: Ensure screening systems do not exclude patients because administrative gender markers do not match organs present.
examTrap: Skipping cervical screening because the chart gender says male even though the patient has a cervix and meets screening criteria.
oneLinePearl: Screen organs and exposures, not assumptions.

title: Disability-Inclusive Care: Ask About Access, Not Quality-of-Life Assumptions
bottomLine: Disability does not imply poor quality of life, incapacity or a preference for less treatment. Ask the patient how they communicate, transfer, position, manage symptoms and want support, and make the environment accessible before judging function or treatment burden.
recognize: Communication disability, mobility impairment, sensory disability and intellectual/developmental disability create different access needs and do not determine decision-making capacity by diagnosis alone.
differentiate: Support needed for communication is not the same as incapacity; baseline disability is not acute deterioration.
assessment: Establish baseline function, communication method, mobility/equipment, caregiver role, pressure/respiratory risks, reproductive/sexual health and access barriers.
workup: Adapt diagnostic procedures to the patient's positioning and communication needs without lowering diagnostic standards.
management: Provide reasonable accommodations, involve the patient directly and include support persons only with consent or when legally authorized.
medicationSafety: Consider altered swallowing, autonomic function, bowel/bladder function and interaction with assistive technology without assuming lower treatment tolerance.
redFlags: New change dismissed as baseline disability
Care decisions made without the patient despite capacity
Inaccessible equipment preventing needed exam or screening
counselling: Ask what assistance is helpful rather than directing questions automatically to a caregiver.
followUp: Document accommodations so future encounters do not recreate barriers.
examTrap: Assuming a patient who uses an augmentative communication device lacks capacity because spoken responses are slow.
oneLinePearl: Communication speed is not decision-making capacity.
sourceBasis: Canadian accessibility and disability-inclusive health principles

title: Newcomer and Refugee Health: Risk-Based Screening With Interpretation Access
bottomLine: Newcomer health assessment should be individualized to country and route of migration, prior health care, immunization records, infection risk, trauma and access barriers. Migration status alone is not a diagnosis and should never be used to stereotype disease or behaviour.
recognize: TB, hepatitis, parasitic disease, nutritional deficiency and interrupted chronic care risks vary greatly by region and lived experience.
differentiate: A refugee claimant, temporary worker, international student and established immigrant may have very different health coverage and exposure histories.
assessment: Use a professional interpreter when needed, ask country/region and dates, prior camps or displacement only if relevant, immunization, chronic disease, medications, pregnancy, mental health and access to food/housing.
workup: Use evidence-based migration- and exposure-specific screening rather than broad 'immigrant panels'.
management: Update vaccination, treat identified infection or chronic disease and connect patients to insurance, settlement, dental, mental-health and community services as needed.
medicationSafety: Confirm medication names and doses from prior countries and avoid assuming brand equivalence.
counselling: Explain confidentiality and health-system navigation without asking patients to justify migration circumstances unrelated to care.
followUp: Track referrals and screening completion because access transitions are high-risk points for loss to follow-up.
examTrap: Ordering every infectious disease test because the patient is a refugee without considering region, exposure or guideline indications.
oneLinePearl: Migration history guides risk; it does not replace individualized assessment.
sourceBasis: Canadian Collaboration for Immigrant and Refugee Health resources

title: Professional Interpretation: Do Not Make Children Translate Clinical Decisions
bottomLine: When language discordance affects informed consent, diagnosis or treatment, use a qualified interpreter. Family members can support the patient but should not routinely replace professional interpretation for complex or sensitive clinical decisions.
recognize: Language barriers increase medication, consent and diagnostic errors.
differentiate: The patient's preference for a family supporter is distinct from asking that person to perform technically accurate interpretation.
assessment: Identify preferred language, literacy, hearing/communication needs and whether the patient wants a support person present.
workup: Use interpreter-mediated history directly with the patient and check understanding through teach-back.
management: Arrange professional interpretation in person, by video or telephone and allow adequate time for consent and education.
medicationSafety: Medication instructions should be translated or interpreted accurately; avoid relying on automated translation for high-risk instructions without verification.
redFlags: Child used to interpret sexual/mental-health or end-of-life discussion
counselling: Speak to the patient, not to the interpreter, and use short direct statements.
followUp: Document interpreter use and language needs for subsequent visits.
examTrap: Using a 12-year-old child to interpret a parent's cancer-consent discussion because the child speaks English well.
oneLinePearl: A family member can support; a qualified interpreter protects accuracy and autonomy.

title: Intimate Partner Violence: Ask Privately, Assess Danger, Support Choice
bottomLine: When IPV is suspected or disclosed, speak privately, validate the disclosure, assess immediate danger, strangulation, weapons, stalking, children and sexual violence, and support a survivor-led safety plan. Do not force confrontation or police involvement unless law or immediate safety requires it.
recognize: Injuries, controlling partners, reproductive coercion, frequent unexplained visits, anxiety and delayed care can be clues, but many survivors have no visible injury.
differentiate: Relationship conflict is not the same as coercive control or violence, though both may coexist.
assessment: Ask direct behaviour-based questions privately and assess strangulation, escalating threats, weapons, stalking, pregnancy, children and whether the patient can safely leave the clinic.
workup: Evaluate injuries and pregnancy/STI needs; strangulation can cause occult airway and vascular injury and may require urgent imaging/observation based on symptoms.
management: Treat injuries, offer advocacy/shelter/legal resources and safety planning, and fulfill child-protection or other mandatory-reporting duties when applicable.
medicationSafety: Consider whether medication access is controlled by the abusive partner and whether sedating medications increase vulnerability.
counselling: Avoid telling the patient simply to leave; leaving can increase danger and the patient is the expert on their safety context.
followUp: Use discreet communication methods chosen by the patient and avoid unsafe portal messages.
examTrap: Calling the partner into the room to discuss suspected abuse and asking both people to explain the conflict together.
oneLinePearl: IPV assessment is private, behaviour-specific and survivor-led.
sourceBasis: Canadian family-violence and trauma-informed care resources

title: Sexual Assault: Consent, Evidence Options, Prophylaxis, and Trauma-Informed Control
bottomLine: Sexual-assault care prioritizes immediate safety, consent for each component of examination and evidence collection, injury treatment, pregnancy and STI/HIV prevention options and trauma-informed support. Reporting to police is generally the capable adult survivor's choice unless a specific legal duty applies.
recognize: Absence of physical injury does not exclude assault and delayed presentation does not eliminate clinical value.
differentiate: Medical care and forensic evidence collection are separate consent decisions and should not be bundled coercively.
assessment: Ask what the patient wants from the visit, immediate safety, strangulation, injury, pregnancy possibility, exposure details needed for prophylaxis and drug-facilitated assault concerns.
workup: Collect forensic samples only with informed consent and within local program protocols; use pregnancy/STI/HIV testing and toxicology based on timing and patient goals.
management: Treat injuries, offer emergency contraception, STI prophylaxis/testing and HIV PEP when indicated, and refer to specialized sexual-assault services.
medicationSafety: PEP and emergency contraception are time-sensitive; do not delay them while waiting for forensic completion.
counselling: Avoid repeated detailed questioning that is not clinically necessary and affirm that assault is not the survivor's fault.
followUp: Arrange trauma, STI/HIV, pregnancy and mental-health follow-up using safe contact methods.
examTrap: Refusing medical prophylaxis because the patient does not want police involved or a forensic kit collected.
oneLinePearl: The survivor can consent to medical care without consenting to every forensic or police step.
sourceBasis: Canadian sexual-assault clinical and forensic practice resources

title: Human Trafficking: Recognize Control Without Confronting the Controller
bottomLine: Trafficking may involve sexual or labour exploitation, coercion, threats, debt, document control or dependence. Create private opportunities to speak, assess immediate danger and offer low-barrier resources without confronting a suspected trafficker in a way that increases risk.
recognize: A controlling companion, scripted history, inability to hold ID/money, repeated occupational injury, sexual exploitation or fear of authorities can be clues but none alone proves trafficking.
differentiate: Sex work is not synonymous with trafficking; trafficking requires exploitation and coercive circumstances as defined by law.
assessment: Speak privately, use a professional interpreter not connected to the companion, ask safety and control questions and assess urgent medical, sexual-health, mental-health and substance-use needs.
workup: Testing follows identified medical needs; do not make disclosure of trafficking a condition of receiving care.
management: Address urgent health needs, offer specialized community and legal supports and follow mandatory child-protection law for minors while prioritizing safety.
medicationSafety: Consider whether prescriptions, phone access or follow-up information could be monitored by a controller.
counselling: Do not promise outcomes the health system cannot guarantee and do not pressure immediate disclosure or escape.
followUp: Use patient-selected safe communication methods and leave access to care open.
examTrap: Confronting the controlling companion in the waiting room and announcing that you suspect trafficking.
oneLinePearl: Trafficking care creates private choice without escalating danger.
sourceBasis: Canadian human-trafficking health and safeguarding resources

title: Virtual Care: Same Standard, Different Information Limits
bottomLine: Virtual care does not lower the standard of assessment, consent, privacy or follow-up. If the diagnosis or safety decision depends on a physical examination, vital sign, procedure or urgent test that cannot be obtained remotely, arrange in-person or emergency care.
recognize: Virtual visits can improve access for stable follow-up, counselling and selected acute complaints but can hide severity when objective data are absent.
differentiate: Convenience is not clinical appropriateness; some patients also lack privacy, devices, broadband or a safe place to speak.
assessment: Confirm identity, location, callback plan, privacy, emergency contact pathway and whether adequate history/objective data can be obtained.
workup: Order investigations and ensure results have an owner; do not substitute a poor-quality video image for necessary dermoscopy, otoscopy or neurologic examination.
management: Give clear escalation instructions and arrange in-person assessment when uncertainty crosses a safety threshold.
medicationSafety: Controlled, high-risk or newly initiated medication prescribing requires the same diagnostic and monitoring rigor as in-person care and may have regulator-specific requirements.
counselling: Explain limitations honestly rather than overconfidently diagnosing through the screen.
examTrap: Prescribing antibiotics for an apparent 'red ear' from a blurry phone image without being able to assess the tympanic membrane.
oneLinePearl: Virtual care changes the channel, not the standard.

title: Consultation and Referral: Stabilize, Frame the Question, Own the Handoff
bottomLine: Referral does not transfer responsibility until the receiving clinician or service has accepted the handoff under the local system. Stabilize urgent problems first, state the clinical question and urgency, send relevant data and track whether the consultation actually occurs.
recognize: A referral can fail through wrong destination, incomplete information, missing tests, rejected referral or patient access barriers.
differentiate: Advice-only consultation, formal transfer of care and emergency transfer carry different responsibility.
assessment: Define why help is needed, what decision is requested, acuity and whether the patient can safely wait.
workup: Complete tests that are necessary and safe before referral but do not delay urgent specialty care for nonessential prerequisites.
management: Use closed-loop communication for urgent referrals and provide interim management and return precautions while awaiting nonurgent consultation.
medicationSafety: Clarify who is prescribing and monitoring drugs started around the referral to avoid duplication or gaps.
redFlags: Critical result with no accepting clinician
counselling: Tell the patient when and how they should hear from the service and what to do if they do not.
followUp: Track unresolved referrals and document consultant recommendations and implementation.
examTrap: Documenting 'referred to cardiology' and assuming the consultant now owns an unstable patient who has not been accepted or seen.
oneLinePearl: A referral is not a handoff until the loop closes.

title: Critical Results: Ordering the Test Means Owning the Result
bottomLine: The clinician or team that orders an investigation needs a reliable system for reviewing, communicating and acting on results, including after discharge or handoff. 'No news is good news' is not a safe result-management strategy.
recognize: High-risk failures occur with imaging addenda, pathology, cultures, abnormal screening tests and results returning after emergency or hospital discharge.
differentiate: A normal result can still require communication when it changes a plan; a critical result requires urgent action and documented escalation.
assessment: At ordering, decide what result is expected, how it will change management, who will review it and how the patient will be contacted.
workup: Avoid tests without a plan for interpretation and follow-up.
management: Use inbox coverage, critical-value escalation, patient notification and backup systems when the primary clinician is unavailable.
medicationSafety: Culture or monitoring results may require medication stopping, narrowing, dose change or urgent toxicity response.
counselling: Tell patients how and when results will be communicated and what to do if they hear nothing.
followUp: Document communication, action and unresolved contact attempts.
examTrap: Assuming an abnormal pathology result will automatically be handled by the specialist because the test was ordered before referral.
oneLinePearl: If you order it, build a plan to see it and act on it.

title: Patient Safety Incident: Treat Harm, Disclose Honestly, Learn Systemically
bottomLine: When a patient-safety incident occurs, first address immediate harm, then disclose known facts transparently according to organizational/regulatory policy, document objectively and participate in system learning. Concealment and premature blame worsen harm.
recognize: Medication errors, delayed diagnoses, wrong-patient events and missed results can cause physical and psychological harm even when permanent injury is absent.
differentiate: Disclosure of facts and apology are distinct from speculating about individual fault or legal liability.
assessment: Assess patient injury, urgent treatment needs, what is known versus uncertain and who should participate in disclosure.
workup: Preserve relevant information and investigate through the patient-safety process without altering the clinical record retrospectively.
management: Provide needed treatment, timely disclosure, apology or expression of regret consistent with policy and ongoing updates as facts become known; report through safety systems.
medicationSafety: Immediately secure medication reconciliation and monitoring after medication-related harm.
redFlags: Patient not informed of material harm
counselling: Use clear factual language and allow questions; do not make promises about outcomes before the investigation is complete.
followUp: Implement and measure system changes rather than stopping at individual education.
examTrap: Quietly correcting an error in the chart without telling the patient that the error caused clinically meaningful harm.
oneLinePearl: Patient safety requires repair, transparency and system learning.
sourceBasis: Canadian Patient Safety Institute/Healthcare Excellence Canada disclosure principles

title: Evidence-Based Practice: Does This Study Change This Patient's Care?
bottomLine: Evidence-based practice integrates best current evidence, clinical expertise and patient values. A statistically significant result may be clinically trivial, biased or inapplicable; assess study design, effect size, precision, harms and population before changing practice.
recognize: Randomization reduces confounding, blinding reduces measurement bias and intention-to-treat preserves benefits of randomization.
differentiate: Relative risk reduction can exaggerate perceived benefit when baseline risk is low; absolute risk reduction and number needed to treat make impact clearer.
assessment: Ask whether the study population, intervention, comparator and outcome match the clinical question and patient.
workup: Examine confidence intervals, loss to follow-up, selective outcomes, funding/conflicts and whether surrogate outcomes matter to patients.
management: Apply strong evidence when benefits exceed harms and fit patient goals; explain uncertainty when evidence is weak.
medicationSafety: Do not adopt a new drug from a surrogate endpoint alone without considering adverse events, absolute benefit and comparator quality.
redFlags: Major conflict of interest without transparency
Composite outcome driven by trivial component
Guideline recommendation unsupported by cited evidence
counselling: Translate benefits and harms into absolute terms when possible.
followUp: Update practice when living guidelines or new high-quality evidence changes the balance.
examTrap: Choosing a treatment because it reduces relative risk by 50% without checking that absolute risk fell only from 2% to 1%.
oneLinePearl: Clinical importance lives in absolute effect, harms and applicability—not the p-value alone.

title: Quality Improvement: Measure the System Before and After the Change
bottomLine: Quality improvement tests changes in a local system using defined aims, process and outcome measures and iterative learning. QI is different from research designed primarily to create generalizable knowledge, although ethics and privacy still matter.
recognize: Useful QI aims are specific about population, metric, direction and timeframe.
differentiate: An outcome measure tells whether health or service improved; a process measure tells whether the intended action occurred; a balancing measure checks unintended harm.
assessment: Map the current process, identify root causes and baseline performance before choosing an intervention.
workup: Use run charts, control charts or other appropriate measurement over time rather than a single before-after anecdote.
management: Use iterative PDSA-style testing, involve patients and frontline staff and standardize successful changes.
medicationSafety: Medication QI should measure safety outcomes as well as prescribing compliance to avoid forcing inappropriate treatment.
counselling: Explain QI changes transparently when they alter patient-facing processes.
followUp: Sustain and remeasure after implementation because initial gains can decay.
examTrap: Calling one staff education session a completed quality-improvement intervention without measuring whether care changed.
oneLinePearl: QI is change plus measurement over time.
